newsitem.title: UK: Pharmacia rules out non-drug disposals - FT.
newsitem.headline: Pharmacia rules out non-drug disposals - FT.

text.p: Troubled Swedish-U.S. drugs company Pharmacia & Upjohn Inc has ruled out selling any of its businesses to concentrate on its prescription drugs operations, the Financial Times newspaper reported on Thursday.
In an interview with the newspaper, president and acting chief executive officer Jan Ekberg said: "We are not trying to sell any of these businesses, we want to build them up."

The newspaper said many investors, dismayed by two profit warnings from the merged group in quick succession, had been hoping to see the disposal of operations in medical diagnostics, animal health, consumer healthcare, contract manufacturing and biotechnology.
There has been speculation recently that Pharmacia Biotech was lined up for sale, possibly to Britain's Amersham International Plc.

Ekberg, who stepped in as chief executive following the surprise resignation of John Zabriskie in January, told the newspaper that management forecasts of $500 million cost-savings by 1998 were "too optimistic."
"We sold too hard both the speed of the integration and its benefits," he said, adding: "I have always under-sold and over-performed. But I think that in the last year we did it the other way round."
Ekberg said the merged company was "not very well equipped when it comes to sales forces...but (in many places) we have two accountancy departments, two personnel departments and so on."

He also told the newspaper that running efficient research and development operations from four different sites, in Michigan, Stockholm, Uppsala and Milan, was difficult, but nothing compared to the inefficiencies of manufacturing sites inherited from Upjohn, Pharmacia and related entities.
Ekberg said the search for a replacement for Zabriskie, whose departure was seen from outside the company as acrimonious, was in its final stages.
The newspaper said he did not rule out an internal appointment for the post. It said most of the top internal candidates for the position were Swedish.
